Stage 01

Pre-Incorporation & Know-Your-Customer

UBO transparency, Apostille authentication chain, official name clearance restricted wordlist, and pre-incorporation statutory fee budget.

UBO Ultimate Beneficial Owner Screening Rules Official Registry Only

>=25% ownership / control

Applicable AML statute: Ley 10/2010, de 28 de abril, de prevención del blanqueo de capitales y de la financiación del terrorismo, as amended (including by Ley 6/2023, de 17 de marzo, de los Mercados de Valores y de los Servicios de Inversión); Real Decreto 304/2014, de 5 de mayo, por el que se aprueba el Reglamento de la Ley 10/2010; Real Decreto 1784/1996 (Reglamento del Registro Mercantil) as to the Registro de Titularidades Reales kept at the Mercantile Registry; Directives (EU) 2015/849 and (EU) 2018/843 as transposed; supervision and enforcement by SEPBLAC, Banco de España, CNMV and AEAT.
Registered Agent & Physical Address Licensed Agent Required

Virtual or co-working addresses are tolerated by the Mercantile Registry only where an identifiable administrative base exists in Spain, namely personnel present during office hours, reception of notifications, and actual location of management. For an ISIC 4661 wholesale marine-fuel brokerage holding a statutory hydrocarbons license and classified as High_Risk_Special_License from an AML standpoint, a mere virtual mailbox or serviced P.O. box does not meet the substance expectations of SEPBLAC, AEAT for excise on hydrocarbons, the energy regulator, and bank counterparties. A physical office with personnel, records and governance apparatus is required in practice under Articles 9 and 346 Ley de Sociedades de Capital.

✓ Partner licensed company-secretary channels provide local registered address and government mail forwarding.

Stage 02

Statutory Formation & Board Resolutions

Competent registry, governing statute, capital lockup rules, and first board resolution template.

Competent corporate registry

Registro Mercantil Central (name certification), Registro Mercantil Provincial of the registered office (enrollment and legal personality), and the Ventanilla Única Empresarial/CIRCE single-window portal for electronic incorporation filings.

Governing statute

Real Decreto Legislativo 1/2010, de 2 de julio, Texto Refundido de la Ley de Sociedades de Capital (Articles 4.2, 20-22, 58-59, 62, 210-212); Ley 14/2013, de 27 de septiembre, de apoyo a los emprendedores y su internacionalización (expedited SL formation, Articles 30-33); Reglamento del Registro Mercantil (Real Decreto 1784/1996).

Formation / constitutional filings

Escritura Pública de Constitución (notarized deed of incorporation) filed with the provincial Registro Mercantil, preceded by a Certificación Negativa de Denominación Social and documented payment of notarial and registry aranceles.

Incorporation processing time

⚡ 50 business days (SOP sum)

Paid-up Capital & Blocked Account Regime Mandatory Capital Deposit & Lockup

Article 4.2 of the Ley de Sociedades de Capital imposes a minimum fully subscribed and paid-up capital of EUR 3,000 for an Sociedad de Responsabilidad Limitada; notwithstanding the metadata flag 'minimum_capital_requirement': false, the statutory floor is mandatory. The capital must be deposited in a Spanish bank incorporation account (cuenta de constitución), evidenced by a certificado de depósito or notarial capital statement, and remains blocked until the deed is registered at the commercial registry.

Funding & unlock path: Fire-safety compliance certificate under the Reglamento de Seguridad contra Incendios en Establecimientos Industriales (Real Decreto 513/2017), supported by an authorized control body (OCA) periodic inspection; structural load clearance via the Inspección Técnica de la Edificación (ITE) of the commercial premises; occupational health and safety plan under Ley 31/1995 with risk evaluation under Real Decreto 39/1997; where petroleum products are stored, a self-protection plan (autoprotección) under Real Decreto 393/2007 coordinated with municipal fire services.

Paid-in capital rule: Article 4.2 of the Ley de Sociedades de Capital imposes a minimum fully subscribed and paid-up capital of EUR 3,000 for an Sociedad de Responsabilidad Limitada; notwithstanding the metadata flag 'minimum_capital_requirement': false, the statutory floor is mandatory. The capital must be deposited in a Spanish bank incorporation account (cuenta de constitución), evidenced by a certificado de depósito or notarial capital statement, and remains blocked until the deed is registered at the commercial registry.

Stage 04

Banking & Treasury Architecture

Central-bank FX diagnosis, tier-1 local banks vs offshore digital EMI matrix, and KYC rejection defense guide.

Foreign Exchange Regime & Central Bank Policy

Current-account convertibility

Spain operates under a fully convertible euro currency regime within the Eurozone. Capital account transactions are unrestricted for EU entities. Current account transactions including trade settlements and service fees are freely convertible at market rates. Profit remittances to non-resident shareholders are permitted after corporate tax settlement and beneficial ownership verification under CRS/FATCA reporting.

Export proceeds surrender rules

Spanish law imposes no mandatory surrender of export proceeds to local banks. Foreign currency receipts must be repatriated within 10 working days. Banks require supporting documents such as commercial invoices and export permits. Settlement occurs at prevailing market rates with full disclosure.

Central bank supervision: Banco de España

Offshore Digital Bank / EMI Whitelist

Cross-border EMI / Fintech rails Fit: High

Low feasibility for offshore digital EMIs due to stringent AML regulations classifying energy commodity trading as high-risk. Spanish fintech platforms impose full KYC and may restrict or prohibit services for oil trading activities.

Stage 06

Corporate Tax & Transfer Pricing

Corporate income tax (CIT), box-by-box return breakdown, dividend WHT, and director personal liability.

Statutory corporate income tax (CIT)

25%

Dividend withholding tax (WHT)

19% Spanish withholding generally applies to dividends and other profit distributions paid by a Spanish SL. Domestic exemptions may apply, including the EU Parent-Subsidiary regime where the recipient is a qualifying EU parent holding at least 10% for the required uninterrupted one-year period and anti-abuse conditions are satisfied. Treaty rates commonly reduce the rate to 5%, 10%, or 15%, depending on the treaty, ownership level, beneficial ownership, and applicable limitation provisions.

Mandatory Return Breakdown

Deadline: · Frequency:

Within the 25 calendar days following the six months after the end of the tax period. For a calendar-year company closing on 31 December, the ordinary filing period is 1 July through 25 July of the following year, subject to statutory weekend and public-holiday adjustments.

Deadline: · Frequency:

Generally 1 to 20 April, October, and December; electronic filing and payment is generally available through the 15th calendar day for direct-debit arrangements, subject to the applicable annual calendar and tax-group rules.

Transfer Pricing & Economic Substance

Master / Local File threshold: EUR 250,000 in aggregate related-party transactions of the same type with the same related person during the tax period is the principal threshold commonly triggering the Spanish simplified documentation exemption boundary. Full Local File requirements may apply below this amount depending on transaction type, taxpayer status, group circumstances, and special rules. A Master File is generally required for Spanish entities belonging to a multinational or consolidated group unless a statutory exemption applies. Country-by-country reporting generally applies to qualifying multinational groups with consolidated annual revenue of at least EUR 750 million.

Economic substance scope: Spain does not operate a standalone, generally applicable Economic Substance Regulation equivalent to the UAE ESR. Substance remains relevant under the General Anti-Avoidance Rule, conflict-in-application doctrine, beneficial-ownership requirements, principal-purpose analysis, controlled foreign company rules, anti-hybrid rules, interest limitation, EU anti-abuse provisions, and treaty interpretation. A Spanish SL trading marine fuel oil and distillates should maintain adequate Spanish decision-making, personnel or outsourced operational capacity, premises or demonstrable logistical infrastructure, risk control, banking controls, inventory and title documentation, customer and supplier management, and commercially justified functions. Artificial conduit entities, circular financing, commissionaire arrangements lacking functions, and unsupported low-tax profit allocation are high-risk.

Fatal Compliance Red Lines & Director Liability

Tax evasion and fraudulent invoicing

Statutory sanction: Administrative tax penalties can generally range from 50% to 150% of the unpaid tax, plus interest and recovery costs. Deliberate tax fraud exceeding EUR 120,000 may constitute a criminal offense punishable generally by imprisonment of 1 to 5 years and a fine of 1 to 6 times the defrauded amount; aggravated cases, including amounts exceeding EUR 600,000 or organized conduct, may carry imprisonment of 2 to 6 years and higher fines.

Director personal liability: Directors and de facto managers may incur criminal liability, civil restitution, tax subsidiary liability, fines, and disqualification from public office or management. Asset preservation, precautionary measures, and judicial travel restrictions may be ordered in appropriate proceedings; travel bans and imprisonment are not automatic.
Value Added Tax carousel fraud and customs or excise evasion

Statutory sanction: VAT assessments, repayment of refunds, interest, administrative penalties, customs debt, seizure, and potential criminal prosecution may arise. Criminal tax fraud thresholds and penalties may apply where the statutory elements and amount thresholds are met.

Director personal liability: Directors may be liable where they knowingly participate, consent, negligently supervise, or facilitate the conduct. Courts may order asset attachment, restitution, management disqualification, and imprisonment in criminal cases.
Transfer-pricing manipulation and profit shifting

Statutory sanction: AEAT may adjust taxable income to the arm's-length result, impose documentation and valuation penalties, deny deductions, apply withholding tax, and charge late-payment interest. Related-party transaction documentation penalties may apply per omitted, inaccurate, or incomplete data, subject to statutory caps and minimums.

Director personal liability: Directors may face tax subsidiary liability where statutory negligence or intentional cooperation is established, particularly after unpaid assessments or improper distributions. Criminal liability normally requires fraudulent intent and satisfaction of criminal tax thresholds.
Withholding tax failure

Statutory sanction: The Spanish payer may owe the omitted withholding, late-payment interest, and administrative penalties. Treaty relief may be denied where beneficial ownership, residence, anti-abuse, or procedural conditions are not satisfied.

Director personal liability: Directors may incur subsidiary tax liability and administrative sanctions where they caused or negligently permitted non-compliance. Personal criminal exposure requires intentional conduct satisfying the applicable criminal provisions.
Shell company, beneficial ownership, and treaty abuse

Statutory sanction: Benefits may be denied under domestic anti-abuse rules, the applicable treaty, EU anti-abuse provisions, or beneficial-ownership doctrines. Additional tax, interest, penalties, withholding assessments, and criminal consequences may follow where fraud is proven.

Director personal liability: Directors and beneficial owners may face tax liability, money-laundering exposure, asset restraint, management disqualification, and criminal sanctions. Piercing the corporate veil is fact-dependent and is not automatic merely because the company has foreign ownership.
Anti-money laundering and terrorist financing

Statutory sanction: Under Spain's AML framework, serious and very serious infringements may generate significant monetary penalties, including penalties calculated by reference to transaction value, profit, or annual turnover, together with public or private reprimands, temporary activity restrictions, and management disqualification. Criminal money-laundering liability may include imprisonment and fines.

Director personal liability: Directors, compliance officers, and responsible managers may be personally sanctioned or prosecuted where they consented to, tolerated, or negligently failed to prevent the breach. Asset freezing and judicial travel restrictions may be imposed by competent authorities.
Sanctions, export-control, and restricted-party violations

Statutory sanction: Administrative fines, transaction nullification, asset freezes, license restrictions, customs measures, banking termination, and criminal prosecution may apply under EU and Spanish sanctions legislation. Penalties depend on the specific sanctions regime and conduct.

Director personal liability: Directors and officers may face personal administrative or criminal liability, asset seizure, management bans, and imprisonment where knowing or reckless participation is established.
Corporate accounting and record falsification

Statutory sanction: Tax assessments, accounting penalties, regulatory sanctions, denial of deductions, and criminal offenses relating to false accounting, insolvency, or document fraud may apply. The company may also lose evidentiary credibility in AEAT, customs, banking, and criminal proceedings.

Director personal liability: Directors may incur civil damages, creditor claims, tax liability, disqualification, and criminal penalties, including imprisonment where statutory elements are met.
Improper distributions and insolvency misconduct

Statutory sanction: Distributions may be recoverable, directors may be liable for company losses, and insolvency proceedings may classify the insolvency as culpable. Creditors, AEAT, and insolvency administrators may pursue restitution and clawback claims.

Director personal liability: Directors may face joint or subsidiary civil liability, disqualification from administering third-party assets, personal contribution to the insolvency deficit in qualifying cases, and criminal liability for insolvency-related offenses.
